specStatements.text: Each colour within the visible light spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction is called specular reflection. Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering: this is called diffuse reflection.
Colour filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths (and colour) and transmitting other wavelengths (and colour).

The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths of light are more strongly reflected. Wavelengths that are not reflected are absorbed. If all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white. If all wavelengths are absorbed the objects appears black.
Objects that transmit light are either transparent or translucent.
Students should be able to explain:
• how the colour of an object is related to the differential absorption, transmission and reflection of different wavelengths of light by the object
• the effect of viewing objects through filters or the effect on light of passing through filters
• why an opaque object has a particular colour.

concepts.definition: The band of electromagnetic waves that the human eye can detect, running from red at one end to violet at the other. It is a continuous spectrum: the colours run into one another rather than being separated by gaps.

concepts.term: Narrow band of wavelength and frequency
concepts.definition: Each colour within the visible light spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency. A colour such as red is therefore not one single wavelength but a small range of wavelengths, with a matching small range of frequencies.

concepts.term: Order of colours by wavelength and frequency
concepts.definition: Across the visible spectrum, red light has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency and violet light has the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency. Because all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum, a longer wavelength always corresponds to a lower frequency.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction. Parallel rays arriving at a smooth surface, such as a mirror or still water, leave it still parallel, so a clear image can be seen.

Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering: this is called diffuse reflection. Parallel rays arriving at a rough surface, such as paper or matt paint, are reflected in many different directions, so no clear image is formed.

concepts.term: Law of reflection in diffuse reflection
concepts.definition: Diffuse reflection does not break the law of reflection. At every point on a rough surface the angle of incidence still equals the angle of reflection; the surface is uneven, so the normals at neighbouring points face in different directions and the reflected rays are scattered.

A material that works by absorbing certain wavelengths (and colour) and transmitting other wavelengths (and colour). A red filter transmits red light and absorbs the other wavelengths; it does not create or add colour.
Light passing through a material and out the other side. Transmitted light is not changed into a different colour: its wavelength is the same on leaving the material as it was on entering.

Light energy being taken in by a material rather than being reflected or transmitted by it. Wavelengths that a filter or an opaque object absorbs do not reach the eye, so they make no contribution to the colour that is seen.

The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths of light are more strongly reflected. Wavelengths that are not reflected are absorbed, so a blue object reflects blue light strongly and absorbs the rest.

If all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white. A white object under white light therefore sends every wavelength back to the eye, which is why it takes on the colour of any coloured light shone on it.
If all wavelengths are absorbed the object appears black. Light does reach a black object; almost none of it is reflected back to the eye, so no colour is seen.

An object that transmits light without scattering it, so light passes through in a single direction and objects behind it can be seen clearly. Clear window glass and still, clean water are transparent.
An object that transmits light but scatters it as it passes through, so light gets through but objects behind it cannot be seen clearly. Frosted glass, tracing paper and thin fabric are translucent.
An object that transmits no light. Light falling on it is either reflected or absorbed, and it is the balance of those two that fixes the colour the object appears.

The idea that one object treats different wavelengths of light differently: it may reflect some strongly, absorb others and transmit others. The colour seen depends on which wavelengths actually reach the eye, so it depends on the object and on the light falling on it.

concepts.term: Viewing an object through a filter
concepts.definition: What is seen depends on which wavelengths the object sends towards the filter and which of those the filter transmits. If the filter absorbs every wavelength the object reflects, no light reaches the eye and the object looks black.

misconceptions.question: Is a colour such as red a single wavelength of light?
misconceptions.correct: Each colour within the visible light spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency, so red covers a small range of wavelengths, not one value.
misconceptions.misconception: Red light is one exact wavelength, green is another exact wavelength, and so on — one number per colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Spectrum diagrams in books print a single value next to each colour, and questions often quote 'red light of wavelength 700 nm', which makes each colour look like one fixed number.
misconceptions.correction: Read the specification wording literally: each colour has a narrow band of wavelength and frequency. The bands sit next to each other and run continuously into one another, which is why the spectrum has no gaps or sharp lines in it.

misconceptions.question: Do all the colours of visible light have the same frequency?
misconceptions.correct: No. Each colour has its own narrow band of frequency as well as its own narrow band of wavelength; the two change together.
misconceptions.misconception: Colours differ in wavelength, but they are all light, so they must all have the same frequency.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet 'visible light travels at the same speed' and mistakenly transfer 'the same' from speed to frequency, treating wavelength as the only property that varies.
misconceptions.correction: For waves travelling at the same speed, wave speed = frequency × wavelength, so if the wavelength band is different the frequency band must be different too. A change in wavelength forces a change in frequency.

misconceptions.question: Which has the higher frequency, red light or violet light?
misconceptions.correct: Violet light has the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength; red light has the lower frequency and the longer wavelength.
misconceptions.misconception: Red light has the highest frequency of the visible colours, because red looks the strongest and is linked with heat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Red is associated with heat and danger, and infrared sits next to red in the spectrum, so students assume red is the 'most energetic' end.
misconceptions.correction: Order the visible spectrum: red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, violet the shortest wavelength and highest frequency. Infrared lies beyond red precisely because it has an even longer wavelength and even lower frequency.

misconceptions.question: Does diffuse reflection break the law of reflection?
misconceptions.correct: No. At each point on the rough surface the angle of incidence still equals the angle of reflection; scattering happens because the surface is uneven.
misconceptions.misconception: On a rough surface the rays just bounce off at random angles, so the law of reflection does not apply.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The scattered rays clearly are not parallel, and students conclude that the rule they learned for mirrors has been abandoned rather than applied point by point.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the normal at several points on a bumpy surface. Each normal points a different way, so identical incoming rays meet different surfaces and leave in different directions — every one of them still obeying the law of reflection.

misconceptions.question: Why can you not see your reflection in a sheet of white paper?
misconceptions.correct: The paper does reflect the light, but its rough surface scatters it in many directions, so no clear image is formed. This is diffuse reflection.
misconceptions.misconception: A rough surface absorbs light instead of reflecting it, which is why nothing is reflected back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'No image' is read as 'no reflection', and absorption is the only other process students can name for light that appears to have gone.
misconceptions.correction: White paper is bright, so it must be reflecting most of the light that reaches it. If it absorbed the light it would look black. The light is reflected, but scattered.

misconceptions.question: Can any surface other than a mirror give specular reflection?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Specular reflection is reflection from any smooth surface in a single direction — still water, polished metal and glossy paint all show it.
misconceptions.misconception: Specular reflection only happens with mirrors; everything else scatters light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every worked example and ray diagram in class uses a mirror, so the term becomes attached to the object rather than to the smoothness of the surface.
misconceptions.correction: The property that matters is how smooth the surface is compared with the wavelength of light, not what the object is called. A still pond gives specular reflection; the same pond with ripples on it gives diffuse reflection.

misconceptions.question: What does a red filter do to white light?
misconceptions.correct: It absorbs the other wavelengths and transmits red, so only red light comes out the far side.
misconceptions.misconception: The filter adds red colour to the light, colouring whatever passes through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The filter looks red and the light coming out is red, so students read it as a dye or a paint being added rather than as a subtraction.
misconceptions.correction: Filters take away. The beam leaving a red filter is dimmer than the beam entering it, because the wavelengths that were absorbed are missing. A filter can never put a wavelength into a beam that was not there before.

misconceptions.question: Does a filter change the wavelength of the light that passes through it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Colour filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others; the transmitted light keeps the wavelength it already had.
misconceptions.misconception: The filter converts the light passing through it into light of the filter's own colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'the light turns red' are used loosely in everyday speech, and students take 'turns' as a change happening to each wave rather than as a selection between waves.
misconceptions.correction: Think of a filter as a gate, not a paint pot: some wavelengths are let through unchanged and the rest are absorbed. Shine pure green light at a red filter and nothing comes out — there is nothing for it to change.

misconceptions.question: What comes out when light passes through a red filter and then a green filter?
misconceptions.correct: No light. The red filter transmits only red light, and the green filter absorbs that red light.
misconceptions.misconception: The light is already red once it has left the first filter, so the second filter cannot take it away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the light as having been permanently 'set' to a colour, and forget that the second filter absorbs every wavelength except green.
misconceptions.correction: Apply each filter in turn to the wavelengths actually present. After the red filter only red remains; a green filter absorbs red, so nothing is transmitted and the screen stays dark.

misconceptions.question: A jumper looks blue in white light. What is it doing to blue light?
misconceptions.correct: It is reflecting blue light strongly and absorbing the other wavelengths.
misconceptions.misconception: It absorbs blue light — the blue is soaked up by the jumper, which is why we call it blue.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that the colour is somehow 'taken' by the object, and absorbing feels like the active process, while reflection sounds like nothing happening.
misconceptions.correction: Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the wavelengths that are not reflected are the ones absorbed.

misconceptions.question: Why does a black object look black in a brightly lit room?
misconceptions.correct: Light does fall on it, but all wavelengths are absorbed, so almost none is reflected back to the eye.
misconceptions.misconception: It looks black because no light reaches it — black objects are just objects in the dark.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Darkness and black look identical, so absence of light and absorption of light get treated as the same explanation.
misconceptions.correction: A black car in sunlight is in bright light and still looks black, and it gets hot — evidence that the light is arriving and being absorbed rather than never arriving.

misconceptions.question: What does a white object do with the light that falls on it?
misconceptions.correct: All wavelengths are reflected equally, which is why it appears white in white light.
misconceptions.misconception: White objects let all of the light pass straight through them, which is why nothing is held back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Lets all the light through' and 'sends all the light back' both mean 'nothing is stopped', so students pick transmission when the object is opaque.
misconceptions.correction: An opaque white object such as a sheet of card transmits no light at all — hold it up and no light gets through. It looks white because every wavelength is reflected equally.

misconceptions.question: Is there any real difference between transparent and translucent?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Both transmit light, but a transparent object lets it through without scattering so a clear view is possible, while a translucent object scatters the light it transmits.
misconceptions.misconception: Transparent and translucent both just mean see-through, so the two words can be swapped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words are used loosely in everyday English for anything that is not solid-looking, and both really do transmit light.
misconceptions.correction: Test it by trying to read print through the material. Through clear glass the print is sharp (transparent); through frosted glass or tracing paper light still gets through but the print cannot be read (translucent).

misconceptions.question: How does a red book look in a room lit only by green light?
misconceptions.correct: Black. It absorbs green light, and there is no red light present for it to reflect.
misconceptions.misconception: It still looks red — the book is red, so its colour cannot be changed by the lighting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is treated as a fixed property painted onto the object, rather than as the result of which wavelengths reach the eye.
misconceptions.correction: The colour seen depends on the object and on the light falling on it. An object can only reflect wavelengths that are actually shone at it, so a red object in green light reflects nothing and appears black.

misconceptions.question: Is white a colour of the visible light spectrum?
misconceptions.correct: No. White light is all the wavelengths of the visible spectrum together, and an object appears white because it reflects all of them equally.
misconceptions.misconception: White is its own colour with its own wavelength, so a white object reflects the white wavelengths and absorbs the rest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: White is treated like any other colour in art and in everyday speech, and paint mixing gives no clue that white light is a mixture of wavelengths.
misconceptions.correction: The visible spectrum runs red to violet; there is no band labelled white. A white object appears white because all wavelengths are reflected equally, and it takes on the colour of any coloured light shone on it.

misconceptions.question: If you cannot see clearly through a material, must it be opaque?
misconceptions.correct: No. A translucent material transmits light but scatters it, so light gets through even though no clear image does.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything you cannot see through properly is opaque, because it is blocking the light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge by whether an image is visible rather than by whether light is transmitted, and 'blocked view' becomes 'blocked light'.
misconceptions.correction: Ask whether the room behind the material gets any light. A frosted bathroom window is bright, so light is being transmitted; it is translucent, not opaque. An opaque object transmits no light at all.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the colours of the visible light spectrum?

options.text: Each colour is one exact wavelength paired with one exact frequency
options.rationale: Textbook diagrams quote one figure per colour, so students read each colour as a single value rather than a band.

options.text: Each colour covers its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states: every colour occupies a small range of wavelengths, with a matching small range of frequencies.

options.text: Each colour has its own wavelength band but they share a frequency
options.rationale: Students who know all light travels at one speed wrongly extend 'the same' from speed to frequency.

options.text: All colours share one wavelength band but travel at different speeds
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think colour must be caused by a difference in speed, having ruled out wavelength.

mcqs.stem: Red light is at one end of the visible spectrum and violet light at the other. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Red light has a longer wavelength and a higher frequency than violet
options.rationale: Students associate red with heat and energy and so award it the highest frequency, missing that frequency falls as wavelength rises.

options.text: Red light has the same frequency band as violet but is longer in wavelength
options.rationale: Picked by students who treat frequency as fixed for all light and let only wavelength vary.

options.text: Red light has a shorter wavelength and a lower frequency than violet
options.rationale: Gets the frequency right but reverses the wavelength, from muddling the order of the spectrum.

options.text: Red light has a longer wavelength and a lower frequency than violet
options.rationale: Red sits at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum, and at a fixed wave speed a longer wavelength means a lower frequency.

mcqs.stem: A beam of parallel light rays hits a sheet of white paper and leaves in many different directions. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Diffuse reflection: the law of reflection does not hold at a rough surface
options.rationale: Names the right process but for the wrong reason; students assume scattered rays must mean the law has been abandoned.

options.text: Absorption: a rough surface takes light in instead of reflecting it back
options.rationale: Students equate 'no image formed' with 'no reflection', so absorption is the only process left.

options.text: Specular reflection: the paper is white so it reflects every wavelength
options.rationale: Confuses being white (all wavelengths reflected) with being smooth (reflection in a single direction).

options.text: Diffuse reflection: the rough surface reflects the rays in many directions
options.rationale: Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering, and the specification calls this diffuse reflection.

mcqs.stem: A wall painted with matt paint shows diffuse reflection. Which statement about the individual rays is correct?

options.text: Each ray still obeys the law of reflection, but the normals point different ways
options.rationale: The surface is uneven, so neighbouring points have normals in different directions and the reflected rays are scattered even though each obeys the law.

options.text: The law of reflection is broken, because the rays leave at completely random angles
options.rationale: The scattered rays are clearly not parallel, so students conclude the mirror rule has stopped applying.

options.text: Only a mirror can obey the law of reflection, so painted walls simply scatter light
options.rationale: Every classroom example uses a mirror, so the law becomes attached to the object rather than to the surface.

options.text: Each ray shares the same normal, so the reflected beam stays parallel after the wall
options.rationale: Describes specular reflection, chosen by students who apply the smooth-surface picture to a rough surface.

mcqs.stem: You can see your face in a still pond, but not when the wind puts ripples on it. Why?

options.text: Rippled water absorbs the light, so almost none of it returns to your eyes
options.rationale: Loss of the image is read as loss of the light, and absorption is the process students reach for.

options.text: Only a mirror is smooth enough to reflect light well enough to form an image
options.rationale: Students tie specular reflection to mirrors alone and so reject the still pond as a reflector.

options.text: Still water is smooth and gives specular reflection; ripples scatter the light
options.rationale: A smooth surface reflects in a single direction, forming an image; a rippled surface is rough and causes diffuse reflection.

options.text: Still water reflects the light but rippled water refracts all of it instead
options.rationale: Water is linked with refraction in other lessons, so the ripples are wrongly explained by bending rather than scattering.

mcqs.stem: How does a green colour filter work?

options.text: It transmits green light and absorbs the other wavelengths
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: filters absorb certain wavelengths and transmit others.

options.text: It adds green colour to whatever light passes through it
options.rationale: The filter looks green and the emerging light is green, so students read the filter as a dye being added.

options.text: It changes the wavelength of the light passing to green
options.rationale: Everyday phrasing ('the light turns green') suggests each wave is converted rather than selected.

options.text: It reflects green light and transmits all other wavelengths
options.rationale: Swaps the filter for the rule about opaque coloured objects, which do work by reflection.

mcqs.stem: White light is shone through a red filter and then through a green filter onto a screen. What is seen on the screen?

options.text: Red light, because once light has left the first filter its colour cannot be removed
options.rationale: Students treat the beam's colour as permanently set by the first filter instead of testing it against the second.

options.text: Green light, because the second filter changes the red light passing through it
options.rationale: If filters convert light rather than select it, the last filter in the line decides the colour.

options.text: No light, because the green filter absorbs the red light the first filter transmits
options.rationale: The red filter transmits only red; a green filter absorbs red, so no wavelengths are transmitted and the screen is dark.

options.text: Yellow light, because the red light and the green filter combine their colours
options.rationale: Students who think filters add colour then mix the two colours as if they were paints.

mcqs.stem: A red rose with green leaves is viewed through a blue filter in white light. How does it appear?

options.text: The petals appear blue and the leaves appear blue
options.rationale: Students who think a filter adds its colour expect everything seen through it to turn blue.

options.text: The petals appear red and the leaves appear black
options.rationale: Colour is treated as fixed to the object, so the red petals are expected to stay red whatever the filter does.

options.text: Both the petals and the leaves appear black
options.rationale: The petals reflect red and the leaves reflect green; the blue filter absorbs both, so no light from the rose reaches the eye.

options.text: The petals appear black and the leaves stay green
options.rationale: Half-applies the rule, correctly blocking red but forgetting the blue filter absorbs green too.

mcqs.stem: What determines the colour of an opaque object seen in white light?

options.text: The wavelengths of light that it reflects most strongly
options.rationale: The specification states that colour is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the rest are absorbed.

options.text: The wavelengths of light that it absorbs most strongly
options.rationale: Absorption feels like the active process, so students think the object keeps the colour it absorbs.

options.text: The wavelengths of light that pass right through it
options.rationale: Transmission is offered even for an opaque object, which by definition transmits no light.

options.text: The wavelengths of light that it turns into other colours
options.rationale: Assumes the surface converts light, the same conversion error students make with filters.

mcqs.stem: A jumper appears blue in white light. Which statement describes what the jumper is doing?

options.text: It absorbs blue light strongly and reflects the other wavelengths
options.rationale: The common inversion: students think the object soaks up the colour it appears to be.

options.text: It reflects blue light strongly and absorbs the other wavelengths
options.rationale: Blue is the wavelength band reaching the eye, so it is the one reflected; the wavelengths not reflected are absorbed.

options.text: It transmits blue light and reflects all the other wavelengths
options.rationale: Transmission is wrongly invoked for an opaque object such as a woollen jumper.

options.text: It reflects every wavelength equally and gives out blue light too
options.rationale: Treats the jumper as a source of light rather than as a reflector.

mcqs.stem: A book that looks red in white light is placed in a room lit only by green light. How does it look, and why?

options.text: Red, because the colour belongs to the book and the lighting cannot change it
options.rationale: Colour is treated as a fixed property of the object rather than as the light reaching the eye.

options.text: Green, because the book reflects back whatever light happens to be shone on it
options.rationale: Applies the rule for a white object, which reflects all wavelengths equally, to a red one.

options.text: Yellow, because red from the book mixes with green from the lamp in the room
options.rationale: Students who think colour is added then mix the object's colour with the lamp's colour.

options.text: Black, because it absorbs the green light and no red light is there to reflect
options.rationale: A red object reflects only red; with no red light present and green light absorbed, no light reaches the eye.

mcqs.stem: Why does an object appear white when white light shines on it?

options.text: Because all of the wavelengths are reflected equally
options.rationale: The specification states that if all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white.

options.text: Because all of the wavelengths pass straight through it
options.rationale: 'Nothing is stopped' is read as transmission rather than as total reflection.

options.text: Because it reflects only the white wavelengths of light
options.rationale: Treats white as a colour with its own band in the spectrum.

options.text: Because all of the wavelengths are absorbed equally
options.rationale: Uses the correct-sounding phrase 'equally' but with absorption, which gives black.

mcqs.stem: A black surface is placed in a brightly lit room. Which statement is correct?

options.text: No light is reaching it, which is why it looks black
options.rationale: Darkness and blackness look identical, so absence of light is offered instead of absorption.

options.text: It transmits all wavelengths, so none comes back out
options.rationale: Transmission is invoked for a surface that in fact transmits nothing.

options.text: It absorbs all wavelengths of the light falling on it
options.rationale: The specification states that if all wavelengths are absorbed the object appears black.

options.text: It reflects all wavelengths equally but only very weakly
options.rationale: Equal weak reflection would look grey, not black; this blurs brightness with colour.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between a transparent object and a translucent object?

options.text: Both transmit light equally well, so the two words mean the same thing
options.rationale: Both words are used loosely for 'see-through' in everyday English.

options.text: Both transmit light, but a translucent object scatters the light it transmits
options.rationale: Objects that transmit light are either transparent or translucent; scattering is what stops a clear view through a translucent object.

options.text: A transparent object transmits light and a translucent one absorbs it
options.rationale: A blocked view is read as blocked light, so translucent is treated as absorbing.

options.text: A translucent object transmits light and a transparent one reflects it
options.rationale: Swaps the two terms, a common slip when they are learned only as vocabulary.

mcqs.stem: Frosted glass in a bathroom window lets light into the room, but you cannot see clearly through it. The glass is:

options.text: translucent, because it transmits the light but scatters it
options.rationale: Light is transmitted, so the glass is not opaque; the scattering is what prevents a clear image.

options.text: opaque, because no clear image can be seen through it
options.rationale: Students judge by whether an image gets through rather than whether light does.

options.text: transparent, because the light still gets through the glass
options.rationale: 'Light gets through' is taken as the whole definition of transparent, ignoring scattering.

options.text: translucent, because it absorbs all the light hitting it
options.rationale: Right word, wrong mechanism: absorbing all the light would make the window dark.

mcqs.stem: A shirt with red and white stripes is viewed in white light through a red filter. What is seen?

options.text: The red stripes look red and the white stripes stay white as before
options.rationale: Colour is treated as fixed to each stripe, so the filter is assumed to change nothing.

options.text: All of the shirt looks red, so the stripes can no longer be told apart
options.rationale: Red stripes reflect red and white stripes reflect all wavelengths; the filter transmits only red from each, so both look the same red.

options.text: All of the shirt looks white, because the filter adds red to the white
options.rationale: Students who think filters add colour expect white plus red to stay light in colour.

options.text: The red stripes look black and the white stripes look red instead
options.rationale: Inverts the filter rule for the red stripes, absorbing the one wavelength that is in fact transmitted.

mcqs.stem: Light from a lamp passes through a piece of blue stained glass. Which explains why the light beyond it is blue?

options.text: The glass turns the white light into blue light as it passes through
options.rationale: Students picture conversion of each wave rather than selection between wavelengths.

options.text: The glass absorbs blue light and transmits the other wavelengths
options.rationale: The absorb-your-own-colour inversion carried over from opaque objects to a filter.

options.text: The glass reflects blue light back and transmits nothing at all
options.rationale: Confuses the rule for opaque coloured objects with the rule for a material that transmits light.

options.text: The glass transmits blue light and absorbs the other wavelengths
options.rationale: Coloured glass acts as a filter: certain wavelengths are absorbed and the rest are transmitted.
